title: God’s wrath is discipline, not passion
source_text: Ὀργὴν μὲν οὖν ὀνομάζομεν θεοῦ, οὐ πάθος δ᾿ αὐτοῦ αὐτὴν εἶναί φαμεν ἀλλά τι παραλαμβανόμενον εἰς τὴν διὰ σκυθρωποτέρων ἀγωγῶν παίδευσιν τοῖς τὰ τοσάδε καὶ τοιάδε ἡμαρτηκόσιν. ὅτι γὰρ παιδεύει ἡ καλουμένη ὀργὴ τοῦ θεοῦ καὶ ὁ ὀνομαζόμενος θυμὸς αὐτοῦ, καὶ τοῦτ᾿ ἀρέσκει τῷ λόγῳ, δῆλον ἐκ τοῦ ἐν μὲν ἕκτῳ ψαλμῷ εἰρῆσθαι· „κύριε, μὴ τῷ θυμῷ σου ἐλέγξῃς με, μηδὲ τῇ ὀργῇ σου παιδεύσῃς με“ ἐν δὲ τῷ Ἱερεμίᾳ· „παίδευσον ἡμᾶς, κύριε, πλὴν ἐν κρίσει καὶ μὴ ἐν θυμῷ, ἵνα μὴ ὀλίγους ἡμᾶς ποιήσῃς.“ ἀναγνοὺς δέ τις ἐν μὲν τῇ δευτέρᾳ τῶν βασιλειῶν „ὀργὴν“ θεοῦ, ἀναπείθουσαν τὸν Δαυὶδ ἀριθμῆσαι τὸν λαὸν, ἐν δὲ τῇ πρώτῃ τῶν Παραλειπομένων τὸν „διάβολον,“ καὶ συνεξετάζων ἀλλήλοις τὰ ῥητὰ ὄψεται ἐπὶ τίνος τάσσεται ἡ ὀργή· ἧς καὶ „τέκνα“ πάντας ἀνθρώπους γεγονέναι φησὶν ὁ Παῦλος λέγων· „ἤμεθα τέκνα φύσει ὀργῆς ὡς καὶ οἱ λοιποί.“ ὅτι δ᾿ οὐ πάθος τοῦ θεοῦ ἐστιν ἡ ὀργὴ, ἀλλ᾿ ἕκαστος αὑτῷ ταύτην δι᾿ ὧν ἁμαρτάνει κατασκευάζει, δηλώσει ὁ Παῦλος ἐν τῷ· „ἢ τοῦ πλούτου τῆς χρηστότητος αὐτοῦ καὶ τῆς ἀνοχῆς καὶ τῆς μακροθυμίας καταφρονεῖς, ἀγνοῶν ὅτι τὸ χρηστὸν τοῦ θεοῦ εἰς μετάνοιάν σε ἄγει; κατὰ δὲ τὴν σκληρότητά σου καὶ ἀμετανόητον καρδίαν θησαυρίζεις σεαυτῷ ὀργὴν ἐν ἡμέρᾳ ὀργῆς καὶ ἀποκαλύψεως δικαιοκρισίας τοῦ θεοῦ.“ πῶς οὖν δύναται ἕκαστος „θησαυρίζειν ἑαυτῷ ὀργὴν ἐν ἡμέρᾳ ὀργῆς,“ „ὀργῆς“ νοουμένης τοῦ πάθους; πῶς δὲ ὀργῆς πάθος παιδεύειν δύναται; ἀλλὰ καὶ οὐκ ἂν ὁ διδάσκων λόγος ἡμᾶς μηδαμῶς ὀργίζεσθαι καὶ φάσκων ἐν τριακοστῷ ἕκτῳ ψαλμῷ· „παῦσαι ἀπὸ ὀργῆς καὶ ἐγκατάλιπε θυμὸν,“ λέγων δὲ καὶ ἐν τῷ Παύλῳ· „ἀπόθεσθε καὶ ὑμεῖς τὰ πάντα, ὀργὴν θυμὸν κακίαν βλασφημίαν αἰσχρολογίαν,“ αὐτῷ τῷ θεῷ περιῆπτεν τὸ πάθος, οὗ ἡμᾶς πάντῃ ἀπαλλάξαι βούλεται. δῆλον δὲ τὸ τροπολογεῖσθαι τὰ περὶ ὀργῆς θεοῦ ἐκ τοῦ καὶ ὕπνον αὐτοῦ ἀναγεγράφθαι, ἀφ᾿ οὗ ὥσπερ διϋπνίζων αὐτὸν ὁ προφήτης λέγει· „ἀνάστηθι, ἱνα τί ὑπνοῖς, κύριε“; καὶ πάλιν φησί· „καὶ ἐξηγέρθη ὡς ὁ ὑπνῶν κύριος, ὡς δυνατὸς κεκραιπαληκὼς ἐξ οἴνου.“ εἴπερ οὖν ὁ ὕπνος ἄλλο τι σημαίνει καὶ οὐχ ὅπερ ἡ πρόχειρος ἐκδοχὴ τῆς λέξεως δηλοῖ, διὰ τί οὐχὶ καὶ ἡ ὀργὴ παραπλησίως νοηθήσεται; καὶ αἱ ἀπειλαὶ δὲ ἀπαγγελίαι εἰσὶ περὶ τῶν ἀπαντησομένων τοῖς φαύλοις, ὡς εἰ ἀπειλάς τις ἔφασκεν εἶναι καὶ τοὺς τοῦ ἰατροῦ λόγους, λέγοντος τοῖς κάμνουσι· τεμῶ σε καὶ καυστῆρας προσάξω σοι, ἐὰν μὴ πεισθῇς μου τοῖς νόμοις καὶ οὑτωσὶ μὲν διαιτήσῃ οὑτωσὶ δὲ σαυτὸν ἀγάγῃς. οὐκ ἀνθρώπινα οὖν πάθη προσάπτομεν τῷ θεῷ οὐδὲ δυσσεβεῖς δόξας ἔχομεν περὶ αὐτοῦ οὐδὲ πλανώμενοι τὰς περὶ τοῦτον διηγήσεις ἀπ᾿ αὐτῶν τῶν γραμμάτων συνεξεταζομένων ἀλλήλοις παρίσταμεν· οὐδὲ τὸ προκείμενον τοῖς ἐν ἡμῖν συνετῶς πρεσβεύουσι τοῦ λόγου ἄλλο ἐστὶν ἢ εὐηθείας μὲν ἀπαλλάξαι κατὰ τὸ δυνατὸν τοὺς ἀκούοντας ποιῆσαι δ᾿ αὐτοὺς φρονίμους.
pass_a_gloss: Wrath (ὀργή) then we name (ὀνομάζω) of God, but we say it is not a passion (πάθος) of his, but something taken up (παραλαμβάνω) for the training (παίδευσις) through sterner (σκυθρωπότερος) methods (ἀγωγαί) for those who have sinned so many and such things. For that the so-called wrath of God and his so-named anger (θυμός) trains (παιδεύω), and this pleases (ἀρέσκει) the Word (λόγος), is clear from its being said in the sixth psalm (ψαλμός): Lord, do not in your anger rebuke (ἐλέγχω) me, nor in your wrath train me; and in Jeremiah: train us, Lord, but in judgment (κρίσις) and not in anger, lest you make us few (ὀλίγοι). Someone having read in the second of the Kingdoms (Βασιλειῶν) ‘wrath’ of God persuading (ἀναπείθω) David to number (ἀριθμέω) the people, and in the first of the Chronicles (Παραλειπόμενα) ‘the devil’ (διάβολος), and examining together (συνεξετάζω) the texts (ῥητά) with one another, will see on whom the wrath is ranked (τάσσω); of which also Paul says all men have become ‘children’ (τέκνα), saying: we were children by nature (φύσει) of wrath as also the rest. That wrath is not a passion of God, but each prepares (κατασκευάζω) it for himself through what he sins, Paul will show in: or do you despise (καταφρονέω) the riches (πλοῦτος) of his kindness (χρηστότης) and forbearance (ἀνοχή) and patience (μακροθυμία), not knowing that the kindness of God leads you to repentance (μετάνοια)? but according to your hardness (σκληρότης) and unrepentant (ἀμετανόητος) heart you treasure up (θησαυρίζω) for yourself wrath in the day of wrath and of revelation (ἀποκάλυψις) of the righteous judgment (δικαιοκρισία) of God. How then can each treasure up for himself wrath in the day of wrath, wrath being understood as the passion? and how can a passion of wrath train? But also the Word teaching us in no way to be angry (ὀργίζομαι), and saying in the thirty-sixth psalm: cease (παύω) from wrath and forsake (ἐγκαταλείπω) anger, and saying also in Paul: put off (ἀποτίθημι) you also all things, wrath, anger, malice (κακία), slander (βλασφημία), foul talk (αἰσχρολογία), would not attach (περιάπτω) to God himself the passion from which it wishes wholly to release (ἀπαλλάσσω) us. Clear that the things about the wrath of God are spoken figuratively (τροπολογέω) from the fact that his sleep (ὕπνος) also is written, from which as if awakening (διυπνίζω) him the prophet says: rise up (ἀνίστημι), why do you sleep, Lord? And again he says: and the Lord was aroused (ἐξεγείρω) as one sleeping, as a mighty one (δυνατός) reeling (κραιπαλάω) from wine. If then sleep signifies (σημαίνω) something else and not what the ready (πρόχειρος) acceptation (ἐκδοχή) of the expression shows, why will not wrath also be understood similarly? And the threats (ἀπειλαί) are announcements (ἀπαγγελίαι) of what will meet (ἀπαντάω) the bad (φαῦλοι), as if one called threats also the words of the physician (ἰατρός) saying to the sick (κάμνοντες): I will cut (τέμνω) you and apply cauteries (καυστῆρες) to you if you do not obey my rules (νόμοι) and so diet (διαιτάω) and so conduct (ἄγω) yourself. Not then human passions do we attach to God, nor impious (δυσσεβής) opinions (δόξαι) do we hold about him, nor erring (πλανάω) do we present (παρίστημι) the narratives (διηγήσεις) about him from the writings themselves examined together with one another; nor is the purpose (τὸ προκείμενον) for those among us who intelligently (συνετῶς) act as ambassadors (πρεσβεύω) of the Word other than to release from simplicity (εὐήθεια) as far as possible the hearers and make them prudent (φρόνιμοι).
pass_b_english: We do, then, speak of the wrath of God; but we say that it is not a passion of his. It is something employed to discipline, by sterner methods, those who have committed sins so many and of such a kind. That what is called the wrath of God, and what is named his anger, disciplines, and that this is the teaching of the Word, is clear from what is said in the sixth Psalm: “Lord, do not rebuke me in your anger, nor discipline me in your wrath” (Psalm 6:1); and in Jeremiah: “Discipline us, Lord, but with judgment and not in anger, lest you make us few” (Jeremiah 10:24).

And anyone who reads in the second book of Samuel of the “wrath” of God that moved David to number the people (2 Samuel 24:1), and in the first book of Chronicles of “the devil” (1 Chronicles 21:1), and compares the texts with each other, will see to whom the wrath is to be assigned. Paul says that all human beings have become “children” of this wrath, in the words: “We were by nature children of wrath, like the rest” (Ephesians 2:3).

That wrath is not a passion of God, but that each person prepares it for himself through his sins, Paul will make plain where he says: “Or do you despise the riches of his kindness and forbearance and patience, not knowing that God’s kindness is leading you to repentance? But by your hardness and your unrepentant heart you are storing up wrath for yourself on the day of wrath and of the revelation of the righteous judgment of God” (Romans 2:4–5). How then can each person “store up wrath for himself on the day of wrath” if “wrath” is understood as the passion? And how can a passion of wrath discipline? Moreover, the Word that teaches us never to be angry at all, and says in the thirty-sixth Psalm, “Cease from wrath, and forsake anger” (Psalm 37:8), and says also in Paul, “You too, put away all these: wrath, anger, malice, slander, foul talk” (Colossians 3:8), would not fasten on God himself the passion from which it wishes to free us entirely.

That what is said about the wrath of God is meant figuratively is clear also from the fact that sleep is recorded of him. As if waking him from it, the prophet says: “Rise up; why do you sleep, Lord?” (Psalm 44:23). And again he says: “And the Lord awoke like one who sleeps, like a mighty man reeling from wine” (Psalm 78:65). If, then, sleep means something else, and not what the obvious reading of the words shows, why should wrath not be understood in a similar way too?

The threats, moreover, are announcements of what will befall the wicked. It is as if someone were to call the words of a physician threats as well, when he says to his patients: “I will cut you and apply cauteries to you if you do not obey my rules and keep to this diet and conduct yourself in this way.”

We, then, do not attach human passions to God, nor do we hold impious opinions about him; nor do we go astray when we set out the accounts about him from the Scriptures themselves, compared with one another. And those among us who act with understanding as ambassadors of the Word have no other aim than to free their hearers from simple-mindedness as far as they can, and to make them wise.

choices.choice: 'It is something he uses to train' made 'something employed to discipline' (passive παραλαμβανόμενον; 'discipline' now matches the quoted verses)
'so many and such great sins' made 'sins so many and of such a kind' (τοιάδε = of such a kind, not 'great')
'is a means of training' made 'disciplines' (παιδεύει is a verb)
'the ready, surface reading' (doubled) made 'the obvious reading' (πρόχειρος ἐκδοχή)
physician sentence reordered so 'as well' (καί) is placed naturally
'wisely act as ambassadors' made 'act with understanding as ambassadors' (συνετῶς), so it is not the same word as 'wise' (φρονίμους) at the end
all ten Scripture citations checked against the verses; LXX Psalms 6:2, 36:8, 43:24, 77:65 converted to English 6:1, 37:8, 44:23, 78:65

LXX renumbering: ‘sixth Psalm’ quotes LXX Psalm 6:2, English Psalm 6:1; ‘thirty-sixth Psalm’ is LXX Psalm 36:8, English Psalm 37:8; the sleep texts are LXX Psalm 43:24 (English 44:23) and LXX Psalm 77:65 (English 78:65). Origen’s first sleep quotation begins ‘ἀνάστηθι’ (rise up), where the LXX verse begins ‘ἐξεγέρθητι’ (awake) and has ‘ἀνάστηθι’ later in the verse; translated as Origen quotes it. Jeremiah 10:24 LXX reads ‘us’ and ‘make us few’, as Origen has it (the Hebrew has ‘me’). ‘Second book of Kingdoms’ is the LXX name for 2 Samuel; LXX 2 Kingdoms 24:1 speaks of the Lord’s wrath and 1 Chronicles 21:1 of ‘the devil’ (διάβολος, Hebrew ‘Satan’). Origen’s point that the wrath is ‘assigned’ to the devil is kept as he puts it (‘ἐπὶ τίνος τάσσεται ἡ ὀργή’). Wrath = ὀργή and anger = θυμός throughout. ‘ἀρέσκει τῷ λόγῳ’ rendered ‘this is the teaching of the Word’. ‘ὁ διδάσκων λόγος … λέγων δὲ καὶ ἐν τῷ Παύλῳ’: the Word speaking through Scripture, capitalised; the following ‘it wishes’ refers to the Word. Possible echo of 2 Corinthians 5:20 (‘we are ambassadors for Christ’) in ‘πρεσβεύουσι τοῦ λόγου’; uncertain, so not cited inline. The physician’s words are a made-up illustration, not a quotation of Celsus. παιδεύω / παίδευσις rendered ‘discipline’ throughout, so Origen’s prose matches the Psalm and Jeremiah wording he cites.
